'''Joseph Melvin Reynolds''' (16 July 1924, [[Woodlawn, Tennessee]] – 11 June 1997, [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]]) was an American professor of physics and a university administrator.<ref name=PT>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.882113|title=Obituary. Joseph Melvin Reynolds|year=1998|last1=Goodrich|first1=Roy G.|last2=Hamilton|first2=William O.|journal=Physics Today|volume=51|issue=1|pages=76|bibcode=1998PhT....51a..76G|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Hearings>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HyDSAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA637|chapter=Dr. Joseph Melvin Reynolds, Physicist, Educator, University Official|title = 1978 National Science Foundation Authorization: Hearings Before the Subcommittee on Science, Research, and Technology of the Committee on Science and Technology, U.S. House of Representatives, Ninety-fifth Congress, First Session, on H.R. 3607 (Superseded by H.R. 4991)|page=637|year = 1977}}</ref> He was a Guggenheim Fellow for the academic year 1958–1959.<ref>{{cite web|title=Joseph M. Reynolds|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/joseph-m-reynolds/}}</ref>

==Biography==
Reynolds attended [[David Lipscomb College]] (now [[Lipscomb University]]) from 1942 to 1944 and then transferred to [[Vanderbilt University]], where he received a bachelor's degree in 1946. At [[Yale University]] he graduated with M.S. in 1947 and Ph.D. in physics in 1950.<ref name=Hearings/> His thesis advisor was Cecil Taverner Lane (1904–1991). As a graduate student, Reynolds also taught for a year at [[Connecticut College]].<ref name=PT/> In the physics department of [[Louisiana State University]] (LSU), he was from 1950 to 1954 an assistant professor, from 1954 to 1958 an assistant professor, from 1958 to 1962 a full professor, and from 1962<ref name=Hearings/> to 1965 Boyd Professor. From 1962 to 1965 he was head of the department of physics and astronomy.<ref name=PT/> At LSU he was promoted in 1965 to vice president of graduate studies and research development, in 1968 to vice president of instruction and research,<ref name=Hearings/> and in 1981 to vice president for academic affairs, holding that position until 1985.<ref name=Papers>{{cite web|title=Reynolds (Joseph M.) Papers|website=Special Collections, Hill Memorial Library, Louisiana State University Libraries|url=https://www.lib.lsu.edu/sites/default/files/sc/findaid/4529.pdf}}</ref>

In 1957 Reynolds was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society.<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=America Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1957&unit_id=&institution=Louisiana+State+University}}</ref> As a Guggenheim Fellow, he spent the academic year 1958–1959 as a visiting professor at [[Leiden University]]'s Kamerlingh-Onnes Laboratory.<ref name=Hearings/> In 1966 he was elected a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Historic Fellows Listing|website=American Academy for the Advancement of Science|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic}}</ref> He spent a sabbatical year from 1969 to 1970 as a visiting scholar at Stanford University.<ref name=Papers/> Using what he learned at Stanford, he helped to establish LSU's gravitational radiation detection program.<ref name=PT/>

{{blockquote|His experimental achievements included the first observation of [[Landau quantization#Magnetic susceptibility of a Fermi gas|Landau quantum oscillation]] (LQO) in the [[Hall effect]] (with Claude Grenier), the first direct measurement of the added mass due to the flow of the superfluid component of helium-4 (with Bill Good and Robert Hussey) and the detection of LQO in the [[Knight shift]] (with Roy Goodrich).<ref name=PT/>}}

{{blockquote|In addition to his academic responsibilities, Dr. Reynolds was a paid consultant for both governmental and private agencies, including [[NASA]], the [[George C. Marshall Space Flight Center]], [[Union Carbide Corporation]], the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]], [[Ethyl Corporation]], and the [[National Science Board]].<ref name=Papers/>}}

Reynolds helped to formulate U.S. space science policies and their implementations. He helped to initiate the space station's microgravity program and supported the [[Gravity Probe B#History|Schiff-Everitt experiment]].<ref name=PT/>

{{blockquote|Dr. Reynolds wed Ruth Anna Heise in 1950. They raised three children; Molly Elizabeth, John Shelby, and Wendy Lee. His personal affiliations included the Cosmos Club in Washington, D.C.; the Southern Yacht Club in New Orleans; and the United States Yacht Racing Union.<ref name=Papers/>}}
